section_summary: These pages trace Japanese plans from 1934 to early 1936 to build a domestic automobile industry through licensing, Japanese majority ownership, and limits on expansion by Ford and General Motors. Embassy reports describe related efforts to reserve the Manchurian market for Japanese vehicles, while State Department memoranda examine whether the proposed restrictions would violate the 1911 U.S.–Japan treaty. The section ends with an informal American objection to Japanese officials and a Department summary of that exchange.

subfiles.title: File note on motor-car production in Japan
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on motor-car numbers and Japanese production plans.
subfiles.summary: Notes an estimate that Japan would manufacture 1,500 cars in the coming year.

subfiles.title: File note on proposed General Motors–Japan Industry agreement
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on Army opposition to a proposed automobile-industry agreement.
subfiles.summary: Records opposition to a proposed agreement between General Motors of Japan and Japan Industry Company.

subfiles.title: The Automobile Industry
subfiles.about: Describes the blocked General Motors–Japan Industry agreement and plans to consolidate Japanese manufacturers.
subfiles.summary: Press accounts say the Army blocked cooperation intended to supply General Motors with Japanese parts. The Embassy reports that an agreement and stock-purchase contract had been executed.

subfiles.title: Division summary of despatch No. 1067
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese automobile-industry plans and their implications for American assembly plants.
subfiles.summary: The proposed policy would regulate production, subsidize Japanese cars, and possibly reserve Manchurian sales for them. American assembly plants seek Japanese partners; the Embassy doubts that Japan's plans can be dismissed.

subfiles.title: Proposed Control of the Motor-Car Industry and Trade of Japan and Manchukuo
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports developing plans to control automobile manufacture and sales in Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes licensing, subsidies, tariff changes, a standard Japanese car, and a possible Manchurian sales monopoly. He details Army resistance to General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler expansion and considers whether Japanese manufacturers could compete. The report warns that these measures could further restrict American access to Manchuria.

subfiles.title: File note on Ford
subfiles.about: Cross-references another Ford-related record; most of the note is illegible.
subfiles.summary: A damaged cross-reference note concerning Ford.

subfiles.title: Economic Adviser’s note on American automobile interests
subfiles.about: Questions whether supporting American technical participation in Japan’s automobile industry serves American interests.
subfiles.summary: The writer doubts that strengthening Japanese automobile production with American technical help benefits the United States.

subfiles.title: Treaty rights and proposed automobile legislation
subfiles.about: Considers whether Japan’s proposed automobile law would violate American treaty rights.
subfiles.summary: After consulting Ward, the writer sees no present basis for representations under Article 7. More information is needed, especially about conditions that might make Ford’s operations unprofitable.

subfiles.title: Cabinet approval of automobile control bill
subfiles.about: Reports Cabinet approval of a licensing bill requiring Japanese majority ownership.
subfiles.summary: Existing output would be protected, while plant or capacity expansion would face licensing controls.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Ford counsel about expansion in Japan
subfiles.about: Records Mr. Longley’s inquiry about Ford’s proposed plant expansion and likely Japanese regulation.
subfiles.summary: Longley asks whether Ford should expand before a licensing law is enacted. Dooman cautions that protection of existing investments cannot be assumed without knowing the bill’s terms and discusses Japanese financial participation.

subfiles.title: Division summary of proposed automobile bill
subfiles.about: Assesses press reports that existing American plants may operate but cannot expand.
subfiles.summary: The writer concludes that Ford and General Motors appear able to maintain current output, though Japanese majority ownership would be required for expansion.

subfiles.title: License System for Automobile Manufacture
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Cabinet’s approval of a bill to license automobile production.
subfiles.summary: Neville says Kurusu confirms press reports that foreign firms would need Japanese majority ownership for new production, while existing operations would be protected. He encloses two press articles.

subfiles.title: New Bill Requires Japanese Control in Auto Companies
subfiles.about: Describes the proposed licensing bill and Japanese ownership requirement.
subfiles.summary: The clipping outlines licensing, Japanese majority control, and protection for qualifying existing operations.

subfiles.title: Foreign Auto Companies to Be Affected by New Law
subfiles.from: The Okuyama Service, translating Asahi Shimbun
subfiles.about: Speculates on Ford’s options under the proposed automobile law.
subfiles.summary: The article describes Ford’s land purchase at Tsurumi and considers withdrawal, continued assembly, Japanese majority ownership, or rapid construction before enforcement.

subfiles.title: File note on Ford’s Yokohama assembly plant
subfiles.about: Cross-references reports concerning extension of Ford’s Yokohama assembly plant.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a report on Ford’s proposed plant extension.

subfiles.title: File note on automotive-industry legislation
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on a possible bill to protect Japanese automobile manufacturing.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a report on proposed legislation for Japan’s automobile industry.

subfiles.title: Automotive Industry
subfiles.about: Summarizes a newspaper report on proposed franchises, privileges, and tariffs.
subfiles.summary: A proposed bill would grant franchises and privileges to Japanese manufacturers and raise duties on automobile parts.

subfiles.title: Division summary of despatch No. 1440
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Embassy’s findings on planned automobile legislation and treaty questions.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes proposed licensing, Japanese majority ownership, protection of current foreign output, and Ford’s refusal to cede control. It flags a possible violation of the 1911 treaty for further legal review.

subfiles.title: Proposed Automobile Industry Legislation in Japan
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s automobile policy, its effect on American firms, and possible treaty objections.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports that licensing would likely hold Ford and General Motors at existing capacity unless Japanese interests gained control. He reviews both firms’ options, Japanese industrial and military motives, and press reactions. The Embassy suggests studying whether unequal treatment of American producers would breach Article I of the 1911 treaty.

subfiles.title: Automobile Manufacture on Mass Production Basis
subfiles.from: Shinsuke Kishi, Department of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.to: R. A. May, General Motors Japan, Limited
subfiles.about: Notifies General Motors of the government’s automobile-industry policy.
subfiles.summary: Kishi sends an outline of planned controls and invites inquiries.

subfiles.title: Essential Points of Automobile Industry Law
subfiles.from: Japanese Department of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.about: Sets out licensing, Japanese ownership, supervision, and protection of existing operations.
subfiles.summary: The outline limits licenses to Japanese controlled corporations, allows current operations at their August 9 scale, and denies retrospective protection to later expansions.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Kurusu on Automobile Industry Legislation
subfiles.about: Records Kurusu’s explanation of the proposed law’s purpose and effect on Ford.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu says the law targets popular cars and is intended chiefly to restrain Ford’s proposed factory. Existing Ford and General Motors production would likely continue, while expansion would require Japanese control. He says Ford had been warned before buying land.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser’s opinion on the proposed automobile control law
subfiles.about: Argues that restrictions on American automobile firms would violate Article I of the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.summary: The writer interprets Article I as guaranteeing national treatment in trade, including automobile production. The memorandum compares the negotiated treaty language and cites a California decision on Japanese trading rights. It recommends informing Japan of the American legal view if the restrictions are likely to apply.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 882 on treaty objections to automobile control
subfiles.from: Department of State; signed for the Secretary by Sumner Welles
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Directs consideration of an informal objection based on Article I of the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.summary: The Department argues that limiting American companies’ output while allowing Japanese controlled firms to expand would deny equal trading rights. It explains the treaty interpretation and authorizes the Embassy to raise the concern with the Foreign Office if the proposal would apply to American firms.

subfiles.title: Proposed Automobile Industry Legislation in Japan
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Ford’s construction plans and a proposed Manchukuo motor-truck monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Ford intends to build its Yokohama factory despite the proposed law, hoping to establish it before enforcement. Neville also relays a press report that Manchukuo would favor Dowa truck chassis and Japan-made buses.

subfiles.title: Proposed Automobile Industry Law
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consulate, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Forwards a newspaper article about doubts over Japan’s automobile-industry plan.
subfiles.summary: Boyce notes that Japanese business figures are beginning to recognize practical difficulties in displacing American assembly plants.

subfiles.title: Auto Industry Law Gets Less Popular
subfiles.about: Reports growing opposition to the proposed automobile law.
subfiles.summary: The article cites market size, foreign expertise, parts costs, and doubts among officials and manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Request to defer treaty discussions
subfiles.about: Asks whether treaty discussions should await the Ambassador’s return.
subfiles.summary: Neville recommends that the Ambassador lead discussions because he will soon return to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Approval to defer discussions
subfiles.about: Responds to Neville’s suggestion to wait for the Ambassador.
subfiles.summary: Approves deferring action until the Ambassador’s return.

subfiles.title: Proposed exploratory approach to Kurusu
subfiles.about: Seeks approval to explore the draft law with Kurusu and mention possible treaty violations.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports General Motors negotiations with Japanese interests. He proposes an informal conversation with Kurusu to obtain details and explain the American treaty concern.

subfiles.title: Department reply on exploratory conversations
subfiles.about: Approves exploratory talks and suggests an oral statement of the treaty position.
subfiles.summary: The Department permits talks with Kurusu and favors stating its treaty objection if the bill matches earlier reports.

subfiles.title: Economic Adviser’s handwritten note
subfiles.about: Questions the value to the United States of aiding American investment in Japanese automobile production.
subfiles.summary: The writer advises against pressing the matter further.

subfiles.title: Informal presentation of treaty objection
subfiles.about: Reports the Embassy’s informal discussion of automobile legislation with Japan’s Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy conveyed the American view that restrictions on assembly and manufacture would discriminate against U.S. firms under the 1911 treaty. The Vice Minister said he had not seen a draft and would examine the matter.

subfiles.title: File note on automobile industry law
subfiles.about: Calls attention to a despatch transmitting the automobile industry law.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to pages five and six of an enclosure.

subfiles.title: Division summary of despatch No. 1631
subfiles.about: Summarizes Neville’s conversation with the Japanese Vice Minister about American treaty rights.
subfiles.summary: Recaps the Embassy’s informal warning that the proposed law would violate Article I; the memorandum continues beyond this section.
